opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that, for a long time, the bottleneck in my own work was me. I'm sitting there, I have an idea, I tweak a hyperparameter, I kick off a run, I wait, I look at the loss curve, I go "hmm," and I try the next thing. That loop is fun, but it's slow, and it's fundamentally capped by how many hours I'm awake and how many things I can hold in my head at once.

AutoResearch is basically asking: what if I take myself out of that inner loop? You set up a small, well-defined environment, like a training script for a little language model, with a clear metric, say validation loss after a fixed compute budget. Then you let an agent run the loop. It reads the code, forms a hypothesis, makes a change, runs the experiment, looks at the result, keeps it or reverts it, and does it again. Overnight. Hundreds of times.

What surprised me is that it actually finds real stuff. Not necessarily earth-shattering, but the kind of improvements I would have found myself if I'd spent a week grinding on it, things like tuning, small architectural tweaks, little bugs or inefficiencies I'd overlooked. And it's doing it while I'm asleep.

So the leverage shift is that my job moves up a level. Instead of being the researcher in the loop, I'm designing the arena. What's the metric? What's the compute budget per experiment? What is the agent allowed to touch, and what's off-limits so it doesn't game the eval? How do I write the instructions, almost like a program in English, that describe how a good researcher should behave? That "program" becomes the thing I iterate on.

And I think that generalizes. Anything where you have a fast, cheap, trustworthy evaluation signal is going to get eaten by this kind of agentic loop. The hard part, and where humans still matter a lot, is the stuff that doesn't have a clean metric: taste, choosing which problems are worth working on, noticing when the metric itself is wrong. But for the parts that do, it feels a bit like going from doing research by hand to running a little research org of tireless interns. It's still early and kind of janky, but the direction is pretty clear to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to take the human out of the inner loop and let the agent repeatedly run experiments overnight, removing the need for the human to initiate each next step.

r002.rationale: It describes the human’s role shifting from researcher in the loop to designing the arena, including its metric, budget, constraints, and instructions, while the agent runs the research loop.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that for most of my career, the bottleneck on research has been me. My attention, my hours, my ability to hold the whole experiment in my head and iterate on it. And the thing that's changed is that a lot of what I actually do day to day in research is surprisingly mechanical once you look at it honestly. You have a hypothesis, you change a few lines, you kick off a run, you stare at the loss curve, you compare it to the baseline, you decide whether to keep it or throw it away. That loop is the core of empirical ML research, and it turns out that loop is very automatable.

So AutoResearch for me is really about taking that loop and handing it to agents. You set up the environment so that there's a clean, fast, well-defined experiment, something like a small training run that finishes in a few minutes, with a single scalar at the end that tells you if things got better or worse. And then you let the agent propose a change, run it, read the result, and keep going. It's basically a hill-climbing process, but the mutations are being proposed by something that has read every ML paper and every GitHub repo.

And the leverage comes from a few places. One is just parallelism. I can only run one experiment in my head at a time, but I can have many agents exploring different directions simultaneously. Another is that it never gets tired or bored. A lot of good research findings are kind of embarrassingly simple things that nobody tried because it was tedious. The agent doesn't care that it's tedious. And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that it changes my role. Instead of being the person turning the knobs, I'm the person designing the search space and the evaluation. I'm asking, what's the right small-scale proxy? What's the right metric? What's the range of things worth exploring? That's a much higher-leverage place to sit.

I do want to be a little careful though. It's not magic. If your eval is bad, the agent will happily overfit to it and give you garbage that looks great on the number. And the agent doesn't have taste in the way a good researcher does, at least not yet. So a lot of the work is still in setting up the problem correctly. But once you've done that, you've turned yourself from a researcher into something more like a research manager with an unlimited number of very fast, very well-read grad students. And that's a pretty exciting place to be.

r001.rationale: The candidate says agents can propose changes, run experiments, read results, and keep going, so the human need not initiate each next step.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes moving from turning research knobs to designing the search space and evaluation, with agents running the experiment loop.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is, I don’t want to just make myself faster at running an experiment. I want to stop being the bottleneck in the experimental loop. If I’m asking an agent to implement an idea, waiting for the result, and then deciding what to try next, every experiment still requires my attention.

With AutoResearch, the idea is to give the agent a setup where it can close that loop: make a change, run the experiment, measure the result, and decide whether to keep it or try something else. Then my work shifts toward defining the objective, making sure the evaluation is meaningful, and giving it a productive space to explore.

That’s where the leverage comes from. You can have experiments progressing while you’re doing something else. But the really important part is the measurement. If your metric is a poor proxy for what you actually want, you’ve just automated getting better at the wrong thing. So I think the human role becomes much more about designing the research environment and interpreting what comes out of it.

r001.rationale: The response says the human should stop being the bottleneck: the agent makes changes, runs experiments, measures results, and decides what to try next without requiring human attention at each step.

r002.rationale: It describes shifting the human role toward defining objectives, designing the research environment, and interpreting results while experiments proceed autonomously.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is, you want to move from asking an agent to do a task to giving it a process it can run. With research, that process is something like: come up with a hypothesis, make a change, run the experiment, look at the result, and decide what to try next.

If you can make that loop sufficiently self-contained, then you don’t have to be there for every iteration. You can set it running and come back to a set of experiments and evidence. That’s where the leverage comes from. You’re spending your time defining the problem, choosing what to measure, and making sure the experiments actually tell you something.

The tricky part is the evaluation. An agent can get very good at improving a number without making progress on what you actually care about. So I think the human role shifts toward designing the environment and auditing the results. You want a loop that can run autonomously, but whose conclusions you can still inspect and trust.

r001.rationale: It says a self-contained loop means the human need not be present for every iteration and can start it running.

r002.rationale: It describes the human as defining the problem, measures, and environment while an autonomous research loop runs, shifting away from hands-on iteration.
